missionPremise: OPS-16 P-319/P-320/P-321 (operator ruling A-212, 2026-09-17). Williamson's production publish run 7b2540c8 completed and retired all 602,050 served node-facets:tier1 rows for 48491 -- 282,569 R-prefixed rows already legitimately retired, and 319,480 numeric rows that were LIVE. The retirement compared served keys against an index that cannot hold the served keyspace, so every numeric node was absent by construction. Two days earlier the same class had taken Bastrop 48021 (92.5 percent) through a different writer, and ENFORCEMENT.md's 'a mass state change refuses before it lands' had stood since then with no control behind it. Nothing watched retired-share per county, which is why the damage had no instrument.
completionPredicate: P-319: retirement is computed per keyspace, a served keyspace with no index of its own keys is unaccounted and retires NOTHING, the run records the keyspace and the count it could not measure, and the Williamson-shaped fixture is proven in both directions (the bare-key comparison retires 319,480 of 319,480; the gate retires zero and names the keyspace) with a genuine retirement on an accounted keyspace still firing. P-320: one declared threshold and one authorisation flag shared by every destructive writer, the publish retirement wired first, every other destructive writer enumerated with what was wired and what was not and why, a crossing fixture refused with nothing written, and the authorised path shown to still complete. P-321: retired-share per county per adapter computed on a schedule, recorded with its snapshot, a move beyond the declared band FAILS the run, and the pre-recovery Williamson state (1.0 retired) fails it by violation. All three are met in-repo; see statusReason for what is not graded.

The gate and the watch open a target's store through the coverage floor's own reader, which sets default_transaction_read_only=on before anything else. No store write of any kind, no retire, no publish, no deploy, no merge, no sub-agent, no lease taken from anyone else, and county 48491 untouched in every store. The retired-share observation table's migration is written but NOT applied anywhere, disclosed in CP2. Everything proven was proven with fakes and fixtures in `npm test`.

whereTheSetDifferenceIs.correctionToTheRecord: A-212 and this dispatch both describe the retirement as a set difference 'against the county's published parcel index'. Read at the pin, the retirement compares against cad_property (the CAD roll at the declared vintage); the published parcel index (txgio_parcel) is what the P-180 account-keyed exclusion and the P-306 coverage floor read, in the same publish path and one layer away. Both statements are true of different comparisons, and the difference matters: a fix that scoped only the parcel-index comparison would leave the writer that emptied Williamson exactly as it was.

The gate as first written asked a CENSUS question (does the index hold rows of this keyspace label) and passed its own Williamson fixture on that basis. The census basis is kept and named separately, because the two need different fixes.

FACTORY ROW (small, and it will bite the next lane that rebases): .github/workflows/ci.yml's ldt-sha-comment-presence step uses `BASE_REF=${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha || github.event.before }}` for the push event. That is correct only while `before` is still reachable. After a force-push (the ordinary way to resolve a conflicting PR here) the pre-push tip is unreachable from every ref, actions/checkout cannot fetch it, and the step dies with `fatal: bad object <sha>` + `FATAL: Command failed: git diff <before> <head> -- cloudbuild.publish.yaml` -- a red check that says nothing about the diff. It cost this lane one red job. The step's own comment already reasons about the null-SHA case; the force-push case is the same shape of hole. A fix (guard the object, or fetch the before-SHA, or skip with a stated reason) belongs to whoever owns that workflow, not to this lane.

It is not this lane's defect and it was not changed; a later row fixing the retirement will have to decide what it does about the neighbour.

fleetMemory.LESSON: A keyspace LABEL is not a keyspace. Two numbering systems can both classify as 'numeric' while sharing no keys at all -- that is what a gate-blocked county IS (a node id and a CAD account number that only coincidentally share bare digits). Every control that asks a census question ('does the reader hold rows of this label') is satisfiable by the wrong namespace; the question that cannot be fooled is the id overlap ('how many of THESE keys does the reader hold'). Measured cost of getting it wrong: the first version of this gate passed its own Williamson fixture and would have let the incident through.

A control that measures the thing BESIDE the thing it protects is the exact failure this lane exists to fix, and it recurs one layer down: P-306 fixed the coverage floor and the retirement step beside it stayed blind; this gate reads the parcel index while the retirement reads the CAD roll. Whenever a control is built, name the WRITER it claims to protect and the READER it actually measured, and state the gap between them in the artifact.

In this repo a module's own error text is the cheapest durable documentation of a comparison: the retirement's basis string names cad_property and its declared tax_year, which is how the table behind an incident was identified without store access. When building a gate, make the refusal name the reader, the keyspace, the count and which basis fired -- a refusal that names only a total cannot be acted on and cannot be audited afterwards.
fleetMemory.DEAD-END: Resolving a conflicting PR by rebasing and force-pushing leaves the CI check `ldt-sha-comment-presence` red on the PUSH event even when the branch is perfect: the push event's `before` (the pre-rebase tip) becomes unreachable, so the runner cannot `git diff` it and the step fails with `fatal: bad object <sha>`. The pull_request run on the same SHA passes, and both diff-bases pass locally. Do not go hunting for a pin-comment problem when the log's first line is `bad object`; and expect this every time a rebase is used to clear a conflict.
